overview: Modern Belarus became independent as the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991. The map begins in 1994, the year of its new constitution and first presidential election, rather than the beginning of Belarusian history. This card follows the republic and its people, including living crafts, learning and the political constraints on public life.

periods.title: Independence and a constitution
periods.summary: The former Soviet republic developed the institutions of an independent state.

periods.title: The presidential republic
periods.summary: Presidential authority grew after the first election; Belarusian society continued through major political disputes.

items.text: Belarusian straw weavers make baskets, boxes, hats, toys and decorations. A material left after harvesting grain becomes a container or an intricate ornament. Modern makers develop their own designs within inherited techniques, so the craft is still changing.

Some makers create pawuks, elaborate diamond-shaped hanging structures. Traditionally these were believed to protect a household from evil and illness. Their protective meaning belongs to religious and folk belief, while the careful geometry is visible in the object itself.

Skills pass from parents and grandparents to younger makers, and through studios, craft centres, festivals and online teaching. Some artisans earn money from their work; others weave as a hobby. A family tradition can now travel through a screen as well as across a kitchen table.

sections.title: Visitors, candles and a shared meal

items.text: During the first weekend of July, pilgrims gather at Budslaŭ to honour an icon of Mary. Some arrive on foot. Masses, a candlelit night procession and a youth prayer vigil bring different generations together for a shared religious occasion.

Local residents welcome pilgrims into their homes and share meals. Families pass on knowledge of the ceremony alongside crafts, customs and cooking. The festival therefore depends on hospitality and household work as well as the gathering inside the church.

Belarus replaced older banknotes during a currency redenomination in 2016. The replacement notes belonged to the 2009 series, despite entering everyday use years later. The year printed on money and the year somebody first spent it can be different.

From January 2017, the 2009-series notes and coins were the country’s sole legal tender. Banks exchanged old money without charging commission, and the National Bank taught cashiers and the public about security features. Paying for groceries also required recognising the new cash.

In 2017, a national resource centre for inclusive education opened at the Belarusian State Pedagogical University with UNICEF support. It trained teachers and other specialists to support children with different learning needs. Better access required practical changes in teaching, not simply a promise on paper.

The centre helped develop teaching and learning materials and share professional experience. Training future teachers also included ways to welcome children with diverse abilities into regular education. These were documented improvement efforts, rather than proof that every child already received the support they needed.

The Russian title of the constitution includes “Республики Беларусь”, meaning “of the Republic of Belarus”. This is an attested Cyrillic phrase in the legal text catalogued by WIPO, here in its 2022 consolidated version. Belarusian and Russian are both official languages.

The first presidential election took place in two rounds in June and July 1994. Alexander Lukashenka won the second round. The vote followed the new constitution, which had introduced the presidency as a central institution of the independent state.

After the disputed presidential election in 2020, largely peaceful protests met a violent response from the authorities. UN investigators documented the crackdown. This political history affected families, students and workers alongside the country’s creative and educational life.

ending.text: Belarus continues as a state. Independence in 1991 and later constitutional changes altered its political institutions; they did not end its communities or cultural traditions. The map’s starting year is a coverage choice, not a founding date.
